name: Manioc and squash cultivation in the Llanos de Moxos
summary: Dated layers at Isla Manechi in the Llanos de Moxos preserve evidence of early manioc and squash use. Excavators interpret the finds as early cultivation.
description: Layers within the anthropogenic deposits at Isla Manechi, Bolivia, yielded a manioc phytolith at about 10,350 cal BP and squash rind phytoliths at about 10,250 cal BP. The researchers interpret the islands as likely garden locations. The squash measurements fall within a domesticated range, while the find cannot establish whether squash was domesticated in this part of the Amazon or brought there.

impact.note: The paper names this region as a proposed centre of manioc domestication, and manioc became a staple across lowland South America and later the tropics (reach 2); cultivation gave foragers a new capability but the evidence is not yet a farming way of life (depth 2); manioc processing methods are its few known successors (generativity 1).

date.label: c. 10,350 cal BP (c. 8400 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The dated Isla Manechi profile contains a heart-shaped Manihot phytolith at approximately 10,350 cal BP. The authors interpret it as evidence of early cultivation.

evidence.locator: Evidence of early plant cultivation, Figs. 2–3
evidence.supports: Reports the Manihot phytolith from the dated Isla Manechi profile.

date.label: c. 10,250 cal BP (c. 8300 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Dated Isla Manechi layers contain squash rind phytoliths at approximately 10,250 cal BP, with sizes in the domesticated range.

evidence.locator: Evidence of early plant cultivation, Fig. 3 and Extended Data Table 2
evidence.supports: Identifies the squash phytoliths and distinguishes their size from evidence of a local domestication trajectory.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The remains are in deposits on an anthropogenic island. Cultivation on the island is the authors’ interpretation. The original planting surface, exact manioc domestication status and the source of the squash remain open.

evidence.locator: Evidence of early plant cultivation and Implication for biodiversity
evidence.supports: The authors note the need for larger samples to assess whether squash was domesticated in situ and suggest island home gardens.

unresolved.note: Species-level and dated sequence evidence is needed to connect Isla Manechi to later manioc-processing sites on the Pacific slope.

research.note: Full manuscript reading locates both earliest crop indicators at Isla Manechi. The study separates human accumulation of organic deposits on islands from the inference that fertile islands were likely cultivation sites.
